Aside from the promotion issue I mentioned above there's a couple of other aspects (that if I don't bring up someone else will):

* If this is not a bottleneck, it doesn't strictly speaking matter (unless for consistency). In some cases using length directly could be clearer.
* The squared  constant may be less clear in some situations, maybe it could be worth considering using `Math.square(8)` (or some equivalent `constexpr`) in some cases.

To be honest, as an optimization guy myself, unless the operation was appearing or likely to appear in a profile, I'm not sure I would change from `length` to `square_length`. The argument for "consistency" has to be weighed against making things less clear.

I'll reduce it to obvious cases (plain comparisons with simple constants, and loops) and put the less obvious cases in a separate branch for the future

For that I'll add a `Math::square` as well for ease of use

Are you even sure that it IS faster? I've made a GDScript demo running 1m randomly generated vectors a and b through `distance_to` and `distance_squared_to` and my results were 57-60ms for `distance_to` and 55-57ms for `distance_squared_to` and that's without the overhead of having to do a multiplication step for just one dependant variable c (simple float that needs to be squared), which takes the `distance_squared_to` result go from 55-57ms to 99-102ms
GDScript is not useful to measure this, the overhead of GGScript is far higher than any difference in the actual operations

True, the overhead of adding an operation is there. however funny enough running 10m operations with just `distance_to` and `distance_squared_to` resulted in consistent 580-600ms for `distance_to` and `distance_squared_to` ended up increasing to 591ms-615ms, and the results are quite consistently being reproduced on my machine.

I don't understand why the more `distance_squared_to` is used it gets more expensive compared to `distance_to` as that makes little sense to me, but it's a consistent phenomenon on my i3-10105f

Also note, at 100k runs per pass the results between the two are consistently within a few percent of each other (and have to be measured in usec) and very inconsistent in which ones are faster

But if you use GDScript the process of the VM is orders of magnitude slower than any other operation here, GDScript is not useful to measure here, but it's irrelevant to this PR, might be worth investigating

I'm not trying to benchmark how fast the operations themselves are, I'm trying to get how the relative performance of the two acts to a point, which when I'm just calling one or the other from what I understand should just be GDScript overhead of calling a builtin function + the cost of the function, and the overhead can be cancelled out when you're calling the same number of functions on both ends

As a final note on that topic, and then let's not clutter this PR with it:
The overhead is so much larger that any difference in the actual operation is drowned out, it's like checking the difference a single ant makes when weighing an elephant, it just doesn't matter

I'd suggest doing any benchmarks in C++, but if you find some discrepancy that's something for a discussion or an issue report

Overhead isn't constant, it can be affected by many factors, and more importantly noise. When the thing you're trying to measure is faster by a few magnitudes than the overhead, noise starts overtaking your actual measurements. 
You may be getting consistent differences as a result of other factors. For example, the order of the test (whether you measure `distance_to` or `distance_squared_to` first) can be significant. Or perhaps one of the functions is in cache more consistently due to contention with other functions.

The takeaway is benchmarks are difficult :)

The thing I was trying to get across is, this needs to be benchmarked pre vs post changes, by stressing the functions changed as the changes are such micro optimizations that they may themselves end up not working as expected, That's all.

Reworked the cases:
* Restored some expressions for clarity
* Added some temporaries for clarity
* Fixed literals
* Excluded some loop cases

Kept loop cases where the starting value was:
* `FLT_MAX`, which we can assume is supposed to not matter
* A value that can be squared within the range of the value
* A starting value that's well defined

Kept the rest for future use

Left as three commits for now for ease of review, first one being simple (cases with a single line, that's a literal, or in one case using a constant), second being cases with either a separate temporary, or a product in the expression, and last being loops

For optimization, I agree that hot paths would matter, and that readability is good here, but these are classic low hanging fruit, where the code should have been written using the square version from the start IMO, this is less optimizing as much as it's cleaning IMO

But any one of these cases are open for discussion and can be removed if it's considered to hurt readability

Unless there's some bad code in some of the actual methods causing some problems the square version is no slower than the original, so I'd say correctness (i.e. the loop cases I've omitted) and readability are the only relevant factors

For importance I'd say any loop with a square root is bad, and any input related code as well

Sorry if we're coming across as dismissive. Benchmarking changes is never wrong, so it's a good idea in principle.
In this particular case we are reasonably confident that the change is not risky due to our understanding of operator costs and compiler optimizations, with the main concern as @lawnjelly expressed being small effects that may not be worth the churn.

"classic low hanging fruit" isn't a very good argument.

How do you know that that you're not falling for the good old quake inverse square root "optimization" that is no longer faster on modern hardware, but is in fact slower?

How do you know that the CPU is slower at doing a Sqrt of a variable over copying a variable to multiply by itself? or is there even a difference in the execution time of sqrt vs pow on a modern cpu with the way they're architected?

If you find data on that square roots are somehow faster than multiplications then please share, but I don't think it's relevant to entertain that hypothetical

But all that would mean is removing some of the cases that involve just a local multiplication of a non-constant, which are a minority of the cases

Let's focus on the readability and correctness

Benchmarking matters, but there are pretty well established ground truths about what is and isn't good practice and performant operations, we also have to consider *all* hardware

using Squared values very often comes at the cost of readability (not always mind you) and isn't worth sacrificing for a good practice that may have gone stale (when were these ground truths last tested to be valid? was it recently, or a couple of decades ago or more?)
Also important to note _all hardware that runs Godot_, as maybe the Core 2 Duo would benefit (but as of SSE4.2 it no longer does), but a 3rd gen i7 would not.

Most often, the change from `distance` to `distance_squared` involves only an omission of the `sqrt` operator, without adding a multiplication. Sometimes, it involves the `sqrt` omission in the critical loop, and just a single multiplication outside the loop. Rarely, it involves an omission of an `sqrt` while adding a multiplication. Only in the last case is the difference between `sqrt` and multiplication speed relevant. If you're interested in practical costs of operators, I'm always happy to recommend Agner Fog's [documents](https://www.agner.org/optimize/optimizing_cpp.pdf) on CPU optimization. The more interesting cases though are the other two, which are safe improvements.

Anyway, this is getting pretty theoretical. As ATS said this is enough discussion for this one PR. Benchmarks are still welcome, but they have to happen from the C++ side for this particular problem.

I'm fully open to removing any readability hurting cases (to be deferred to a future where we add `Math::square`, which I'm testing a bit)

It'd be worth also looking at moving other code where relevant, but most modern compilers will fix that (including repeated multiplications of the same value)
